questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted my study destination to offer a city with a rich history, as well as a cultural environment that felt completely foreign to me

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I rate my study abroad experience a 9/10. Being in Kyoto itself, as well as the relationships I was able to forge with others, was an 11/10. I rate the study abroad experience itself a 9/10 because the curriculum felt a bit ineffective at times.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, the SKP staff is super helpful. It's a bit annoying, to do all the paperwork, but staff and students alike are willing to help.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I missed my orientation, so most assistance was 1:1 to help me catch up. Assistance from Mr. Murakami, the landlord of the Freepia apartments, was definitely present. He offered food, maps, and 1:1 guidance. He was a very helpful resource throughout my entire time in Kyoto.

Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Organizing my housing via the Freepia apartments was very helpful. Mr. Murakami owns 3 buildings nearby Ritsumeikan University, hosting mainly students. As someone who wanted some privacy (aka not living in a dorm) but didn't feel confident enough to find housing in Japan on my own, I wholeheartedly recommend this living experience. Ritsumeikan decided to invest more in dorms and thus may no longer act as the bridge between Mr. Murakami's accommodation and the students, however this done not mean that this option is not available for those who are interested. To learn more, you can check out this document I made to spread the word about the Freepia apartments!
https://docs.google.com/document/d/1OMG1AdI7XksY6hkJSE9v46_A0lHSyTIGfZnZ12T1xXw/edit?usp=sharing

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I loved living off campus; the freepia apartments (highly recommend) were a 25 min walk/12 min bus or bike ride to campus. However, for living near Ritsumeikan and getting around Kyoto, I would recommend you either 1) get a bike or 2) be prepared to sometimes spend an hour to get to the center of town or to a neighborhood across town. The metro doesn't go everywhere, and more likely than not, you'll be taking the bus as a mode of transport. Busses are relatively small, can get packed, and are pretty damn slow. So if you're living near RU, especially if your accomodation is west of RU (meaning even further from center of town), you may have to either accept long commutes or invest in a bike. You may run into former students looking to get rid of their bikes - that is how I found mine. Otherwise, there are plenty of used bike shops. If you don't mind a slightly longer commute to school but better localisation in the city, look for accomodation (whether its dorms or private apts) that are east or south of RU.

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Pretty standard registration process. The only thing that is a bit of a bummer (if you are going on exchange as a master's student, like me) is that the minimum credits needed from KU do not match the minimum credits needed from RU. So, I had to take 3 extra classes - that didn't count for KU credit - in order to be considered a full-time student at RU (which was needed to participate in the exchange). I ended up enrolling in beginner japanese language classes, and it was actually enjoyable (most of the time) to be able to learn about the content without being too worried about the grades (since the credit didn't count toward my home institution). It did represent an additional time commitment though.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The classes were interesting, for the most part, but I found the processes to be a bit on the lazy and micro-managing side. For example, attendance was taken and daily homework was sometimes given. Additionally, many of the class formats (again, at the master's level) would be the students giving a presentation to the other students while the professor listened. Sometimes we'd have "discussion" afterwards. Some teachers really did not do a whole lot of teaching. I found this unfortunate because I came to be taught by the professor, not by other international students who barely know the subject

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: described above

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Japanese language, migration studies, public diplomacy, local and regional development, global peace studies

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend global peace studies as well as public diplomacy. Peace studies is taught by professor Kimijima, who is passionate about his work, and includes a field trip to the on-campus Kyoto Museum for World Peace, which I highly, highly enjoyed. The homework is extremely minimal (only 2 essays for the entire semester) and it's easy to just sit back and listen to Prof Kimijima lecture. 
Public Diplomacy was equally interesting, and was taught by an American professor named Nathaniel Smith. A trained anthropologist and very knowledgable person, it was a pleasure to be part of his class. The workload was a bit on the heavier side though, with weekly discussion posts stemming from the readings of numerous academic articles in international relations. It was do-able though

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Gas and electric were not included in my rent, but this didn't come back too expensive, it was just a task to go pay the bills in-person every month (though made easier by the fact that you can do it at any convenience store)

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food and rent is incredibly inexpensive, especially compared to Copenhagen. This was amazing. Transporation was a bit expensive, considering the cost of other things, but that's why ended up primarily using a bike (also I just prefer to)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Be sure to check out the "Circles" at Ritsumeikan! These are the clubs and students orgs. I emailed a bunch of them. It's a great way to meet other japanese (and non-japanese) people

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: pottery club, horseback riding, hiking were a few that interested me. there is a very long list of other clubs that are available though

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go out to eat by yourself in Kyoto; go to music events; become a regular at your neighborhood market or grocery store or cafe. Creating relationships with Japanese people, deepening my understanding of the culture and history through its food and its crafts, was one of the most rewarding and wonderful experiences

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend you go wwoofing (volunteering on a farm) before you go back home. Super cool way to check out rural Japan. 
During weekends in Kyoto, do yourself a favor and check out any of the numerous craft markets. You can check the online calendar "what's up in kyoto"
Tokyo and Osaka are cool and all, but there are many riches to be found in less conventional destinations.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Relatively easy given that it was not my first time living in a foreign culture

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join clubs, do things on your own (allowing people to approach you), invite people out to get coffee

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The bureaucracy of the outdated processes, the indirect communication

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: THE FOOD, the generosity, the thoughtful service, the safety, the cleanliness, the attachment to animistic spiritual traditions, the old temples and shrines on every corner

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: consider living in the freepia apartments, don't only socialize with other westerners, be active in your search for events to participate in and attend. oh, and get a bike.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: listed above

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: building friendships with locals

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: my long-distance relationship (tmi?)
